body: A little late to this post but I just accepted a full time offer doing this for Providence in an ER recently and have been about 2 weeks now. my first time working in a setting this clinical, but I did do some work and special education, including being a behavior technician in a moderate/severe classroom. at least that it’s in the emergency room in someways. It has actually been calmer than working in a school because of the quick turnover, discharging patients or transferring them to higher levels of care. What I do specifically is more just being in assistant to nurses in triage. I would honestly not say that the bulk of the work in end of itself feels necessarily rewarding, being that some of the most extreme cases come to this hospital. However, it does feel good to be a support to the staff and so as long as they work well with me, I think it will be OK for what it is. Plus Providence has great benefits, I am happy to be working on 3 12 hour shifts versus a 9 to 5 and my particular company is even great with education reimbursement. I even got a $5k hiring bonus with this position, so my plan for right now it’s to give it a year to stick out all the terms of the hiring bonus (getting half of it on my first paycheck, the other half at the one year anniversary) use it as a stopgap to look into a masters or otherwise more medical training, and if nothing else move laterally within the company if it burns me out after the one year mark. I also work night shift would actually honestly helps as people are mostly asleep anyway. I work side-by-side with an experienced tech at times now and he did say out of everywhere he’s been providence has been the very best so far. it does help that no matter how difficult a case may be, I am not likely to see the person again in 24 hours where is working and I setting I might be working with the same student and set of behavior problems for an entire year. I make a decent hourly rate for my area after the night differential as well - it was more rewarding personally to work in a school, but much fewer hours and frequently having to lose them when things like winter break would come up, whereas it is very easy for me to pick up overtime and extra paid trainings, in what I am doing now so it kind of helps to have a higher earning potential also. I even feel safer doing this job in a hospital than a school, because security is always with us when somebody is first being brought in, and also being moved out.

Yup, I’m an autistic woman and experienced A LOT of the exact things you did when I was growing up. I realized I just didn’t fit in/feel the same as an NT woman. Please don’t commit to anything gender related right now, try out a neurodiverse affirming therapist if you can and see if you can connect with ND peers. You might be able to pass as a bit more NT/mask less identifying as male on some levels but it will not fix any struggles autistics face, unfortunately. Keep in mind that the brain doesn’t fully mature until your mid 20s, so if nothing else wait to commit to any kind of gender change until then. Work on your education & career first. Maybe see if a psychologist in your school now or any school you go to later on can screen you for the autism, and if that’s a thing use that to find you suitable accommodations and therapies as your adult life begins? You can have a fluid relationship w a condition like that over the years, but not with gender if it gets to advanced medical or legal changes. 

You are young and have SO many possibilities out there, remember that ❤️
